title: Case Study: Tic-Tac-Toe
summary: Design Tic-Tac-Toe like an interviewer expects — entities, an N x N board, efficient win detection, and room for an AI player.

blocks.markdown:
**Tic-Tac-Toe** is a classic LLD warm-up — small enough to finish in 30 minutes, rich enough to test **extensibility**: can your design grow from a 3x3 board to N x N, or swap a human player for an AI, without a rewrite?

- Two players alternate placing a symbol on a shared grid.
- The interviewer is grading your **class boundaries**, not your tic-tac-toe skills.
- Treat board size and player type as things that must change later.

blocks.subTitle: Requirements
blocks.markdown:
Functional requirements to design against.

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| Players | Exactly 2, alternate turns |
| Board | N x N, size configurable |
| End state | Win (row/col/diagonal) or draw (full board) |
| Extension | Optional AI player |

Nothing here says "3x3" — bake that assumption in and the design fails the follow-up question.

Pull nouns and verbs from the requirements and turn them into classes.

- **Board** — owns the grid of cells, knows how to place a move and check bounds.
- **Cell** — one square; empty or holding a piece.
- **PlayingPiece** — the symbol (X or O) a player marks with.
- **Player** — a participant with a name and a piece.
- **Game** — orchestrates turns, calls the win-check, decides when it's over.

Each class owns exactly one responsibility — that split is what the interviewer is probing for.

Before code, sketch how the classes connect.

<<< Image: clean UML-style class diagram, blue/grey palette, generous whitespace. Boxes: 'Game' (composes 'Board', has List<Player>), 'Board' (composes grid of 'Cell'), 'Cell' (has 'PlayingPiece'), 'Player' (has one 'PlayingPiece', optional 'PlayerStrategy'), 'PlayingPiece' (enum X/O). Arrows show composition (filled diamond) from Game to Board and Board to Cell, association from Player to PlayingPiece. Minimal text, short labels only. >>>

- **Composition**: Board owns Cells — they can't outlive it. Game owns the Board.
- **Association**: Player merely references a PlayingPiece — many players could share the same symbol type.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: PlayingPiece & Cell
blocks.markdown:
```text
enum PlayingPiece:
    X
    O

class Cell:
    row
    col
    piece = null          // null = empty

    method isEmpty():
        return this.piece == null

    method setPiece(piece):
        if not this.isEmpty():
            throw IllegalStateError("cell already occupied")
        this.piece = piece
```

An enum for the symbol keeps "X" and "O" out of raw strings — the compiler catches typos a string can't.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: Board
blocks.markdown:
```text
class Board:
    size                  // N, board is size x size
    grid                  // size x size array of Cell
    filledCount = 0

    constructor(size):
        this.size = size
        this.grid = build size x size grid of new Cell(row, col)

    method placeMove(row, col, piece):
        if row < 0 or row >= size or col < 0 or col >= size:
            throw InvalidMoveError("out of bounds")
        grid[row][col].setPiece(piece)      // throws if occupied
        filledCount += 1

    method isFull():
        return filledCount == size * size
```

`size` lives on the Board, not hardcoded as 3 — that one field is what makes N x N free.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: Player
blocks.markdown:
```text
class Player:
    name
    piece                 // PlayingPiece this player marks with
    strategy               // PlayerStrategy — human input or AI

    constructor(name, piece, strategy):
        this.name = name
        this.piece = piece
        this.strategy = strategy

    method getMove(board):
        return this.strategy.decideMove(board, this.piece)
```

Player never decides *how* to pick a move — it delegates to `strategy`. That indirection is what lets a human and an AI share one class.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: Game turn loop
blocks.markdown:
```text
class Game:
    board
    players               // list of 2 Players
    currentIndex = 0

    constructor(size, players):
        this.board = new Board(size)
        this.players = players

    method play():
        while true:
            current = players[currentIndex]
            move = current.getMove(board)          // (row, col)
            board.placeMove(move.row, move.col, current.piece)

            if checkWin(board, move, current.piece):
                announce(current.name + " wins")
                return
            if board.isFull():
                announce("draw")
                return

            currentIndex = (currentIndex + 1) % players.size()
```

The loop only knows *whose turn it is* and *when to stop* — win logic and move logic both live elsewhere.

The naive win check rescans every row, column, and both diagonals after each move — **O(N)** work per move just to confirm a line, and it still has to loop over N lines.

- Only the row, column, and (if applicable) diagonal **through the last move** can possibly have just completed.
- Checking just those cuts the work from scanning the whole board to a handful of lines.
- An even better approach avoids re-scanning cells entirely — see the counter trick next.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: O(1) counters
blocks.markdown:
```text
// Maintained on the Board, updated inside placeMove — not recomputed.
rowCount[N], colCount[N]     // signed running totals per line
diagCount, antiDiagCount     // signed running totals for both diagonals

method recordMove(row, col, piece):
    delta = (piece == X) ? 1 : -1
    rowCount[row] += delta
    colCount[col] += delta
    if row == col:
        diagCount += delta
    if row + col == size - 1:
        antiDiagCount += delta

method checkWin(row, col):
    return abs(rowCount[row]) == size
        or abs(colCount[col]) == size
        or abs(diagCount) == size
        or abs(antiDiagCount) == size
```

Each move updates a few counters in **O(1)** and win-check is a handful of comparisons — no cell scanning at all, and it scales to any N.

The requirement says the game may need an **AI opponent** later. Hardcoding "read from console" inside `Player` blocks that.

- Pull move-selection out into a **PlayerStrategy** interface with one method: `decideMove(board, piece)`.
- `HumanStrategy` reads console/UI input; `RandomAIStrategy` or `MinimaxStrategy` computes one instead.
- `Player` holds a `strategy` reference and never checks "am I human or AI" — that branch disappears entirely.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: PlayerStrategy
blocks.markdown:
```text
interface PlayerStrategy:
    method decideMove(board, piece) -> (row, col)

class HumanStrategy implements PlayerStrategy:
    method decideMove(board, piece):
        return readMoveFromInput()          // e.g. UI click or console read

class RandomAIStrategy implements PlayerStrategy:
    method decideMove(board, piece):
        empties = board.emptyCells()
        return pickRandom(empties)

// usage — same Player class, different behavior plugged in
human = new Player("Alice", X, new HumanStrategy())
bot   = new Player("Bot", O, new RandomAIStrategy())
```

Swapping `RandomAIStrategy` for a `MinimaxStrategy` later touches zero lines in `Player` or `Game`.

Two patterns carry this design, both covered in [behavioral-patterns-i](behavioral-patterns-i).

- **Strategy** — `PlayerStrategy` swaps human vs AI move logic without touching `Player` or `Game`.
- **Factory** (optional) — a `PlayerFactory` can build the right `Player` + `strategy` pair from a config flag, keeping construction logic out of `Game`.

The same skeleton — Board of Cells, Player with a Strategy, Game driving turns — generalizes directly.

blocks.subTitle: Beyond 3x3
blocks.markdown:
How the same classes stretch to related games.

| Game | What changes |
|---|---|
| Connect-Four | Moves drop into a column; win-check adds gravity, not new classes |
| Chess | Cell holds a `Piece` type + owner; win-check becomes check/checkmate rules |

Board, Cell, and Player stay put — only the move rule and win rule are swapped.

Cases interviewers probe for:

- **Invalid move** — out-of-bounds or an already-occupied cell must throw/reject, not silently overwrite.
- **Full board, no winner** — `isFull()` must be checked *after* the win check each turn, or a draw masks a winning last move.
- **Extensions** — undo/redo (store a move stack), replay, or a network multiplayer mode all slot in without touching `Board`'s core logic.

blocks.subTitle: Efficient win check
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you check for a win efficiently?**

Don't rescan the whole board. Maintain a signed running counter per row, per column, and per diagonal, updated by ±1 as each piece is placed. After a move, a win is just `abs(counter) == size` for the row/col/diagonal that move touched — O(1) per move instead of O(N) per check, and it scales to any board size.

blocks.subTitle: Configurable board size
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you make the board size configurable?**

Store `size` as a field on `Board`, pass it into the constructor, and size every array (`grid`, `rowCount`, `colCount`) off that field instead of a literal 3. The win-check counters and `isFull()` already work off `size`, so N x N falls out of the same code that handles 3x3 — no branching on board dimensions anywhere.

blocks.subTitle: Human vs AI pattern
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Which pattern lets you support both a human and an AI player?**

Strategy. Define a `PlayerStrategy` interface with `decideMove(board, piece)`, and give `Player` a `strategy` field instead of hardcoded input logic. `HumanStrategy` reads user input, `MinimaxStrategy` computes one. `Player` and `Game` stay unchanged when you add a new strategy — that's the open/closed principle in action, from [behavioral-patterns-i](behavioral-patterns-i).

blocks.subTitle: Extending to Connect-Four
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How would you extend this design to Connect-Four?**

Keep `Board`, `Cell`, `Player`, and `Game`'s turn loop as-is. Change the move rule so a placed piece "drops" to the lowest empty cell in a chosen column rather than an arbitrary (row, col). The win-check counters still work per row/column/diagonal — you're only swapping the move-placement rule, which is exactly the kind of change this class split was built to isolate. For the walking-through-a-design method itself, see [lld-interview-framework](lld-interview-framework).
